title: Distribution, Supply Chain and Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Cheniere is a full-service LNG provider, with capabilities that include gas procurement and transportation, liquefaction, vessel chartering, and LNG delivery.
epigraph.author: Cheniere Energy, 2026 third-quarter release [3]

web_blocks.text: Cheniere does not sell LNG through retail outlets, dealers or a software-style reseller channel. Its go-to-market is direct, contract-led B2B selling through Cheniere Marketing and the terminal subsidiaries. The core customer instruments are long-term SPAs; spot and other short- or medium-term sales handle uncontracted production and trading opportunities. Some agreements are arranged with creditworthy utilities, portfolio companies, national energy firms and other LNG buyers. The seller's commercial team negotiates volume, delivery window, duration, cost allocation, fees, transfer point, cancellation rights, destination flexibility and credit protection. Contract terms differ; the 2025 Form 10-K describes the overall structures rather than publishing every confidential SPA. [2]

The supply chain starts upstream of the terminal. Cheniere buys natural gas from a network of producers and holds pipeline transportation capacity to move that gas to Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi. Sabine Pass has multiple interstate and intrastate connections and access to supply east of the Rocky Mountains; Corpus Christi's system connects to supply regions including the Permian. The company also has long-term transportation agreements. Pipeline access is a strategic input, not a decorative convenience: a liquefaction plant cannot run at design rates if gas is unavailable, a connection is constrained or transport capacity fails. [2][4][5]

At the terminal, gas is conditioned and passed through a train's refrigeration system. Cooling turns gas into a liquid at cryogenic temperature and compresses its volume to about one-six-hundredth of the gaseous state. Liquefaction consumes fuel and power; equipment must be maintained; and LNG is buffered in tanks before marine loading. Berths, loading arms, channel access, storage and pipeline redundancy each impose their own operating limits. The shipment calendar must match production, vessel arrival windows, export approvals and customer nominations. [2][4][5]

web_blocks.title: Contract economics: distinguish the gas molecule from the liquefaction service

web_blocks.text: Cheniere's 2025 Form 10-K describes long-term SPAs with fixed fees on contracted volumes, generally payable even if a buyer elects not to lift or suspends a cargo, subject to the contract. It also describes a variable fee that is primarily indexed to Henry Hub and is generally structured to cover gas purchases, transportation and liquefaction fuel. This combination gives the seller a fixed-fee component and a feed-gas pass-through, while leaving important contract, fuel, transport, basis, credit and operating details to the actual agreement. Do not transfer one SPA's terms to another. [2]

IPM agreements work differently. In the Form 10-K description, a gas producer sells gas to Cheniere on a global LNG or natural-gas index basis, less fixed liquefaction, shipping and other costs; the linked sale of LNG and purchase of gas can expose Cheniere to timing and index movements. Derivatives may hedge economic exposures, but accounting can recognize fair-value changes before physical delivery. This explains why a long-term contract book can stabilize a portion of expected commercial cash flow while reported earnings remain volatile. [2][3]

web_blocks.text: Petrobras illustrates the FOB chain without requiring a made-up contract price. Its public SPA states 0.8 mtpa and a 22-year term. Once Cheniere Marketing has procured gas, transported it to a facility and loaded the LNG, Petrobras takes delivery at the U.S. terminal and manages shipping to its receiving system. Petrobras says this kind of long-term commitment helps reduce reliance on the spot market and strengthens supply flexibility. Cheniere's release calls the agreement commercial support for future brownfield expansion, but that does not mean the contract's economics or realized margin are public. [3][13]

FOB and delivered contracts can create different timing between loading, control transfer, delivery, invoicing and cash collection. For a delivered cargo, the ship may still be at sea at period end; Cheniere reported 61 TBtu of LNG sold on a delivered basis in transit at September 30, 2026. Its 10-K also reports contract assets arising primarily from SPAs with tiered payment structures: the company may have transferred goods or services and recognized a right to consideration before that consideration is due. Contract assets were $424 million at December 31, 2025, compared with $331 million a year earlier. [2][3]

The company did not publish a verified days-sales-outstanding figure in the evidence used here, so I will not manufacture one from annual revenue and a period-end receivable balance. Nor does the absence of a customer representing 10% of annual revenue mean collection exposure is evenly distributed: at December 31, 2025, one customer represented 15% of combined trade receivables and contract assets. The practical monitoring question is whether invoiced balances, contract assets, collateral postings, deferred revenue and cash receipts move in line with cargo delivery and the contracted payment schedule. [2]

web_blocks.text: The revenue-to-cash path is not simply invoice, then collection. Under a tiered SPA payment schedule, Cheniere can recognize a contract asset when the customer consideration is not yet due; deferred revenue captures cash or consideration received before the related performance obligation is satisfied. Margin deposits and derivative balances can also move with market exposure and contract timing. These are not all routine trade receivables, so a simple receivable-to-revenue ratio would combine different economic items. The 2025 Form 10-K describes the categories and the tiered-payment origin of contract assets but does not publish a DSO series. [2]

At the portfolio level, Cheniere says it aims to contract about 90% of current and planned liquefaction capacity under long-term SPAs and IPM agreements. Contracting future output may help support financing and de-risk the demand side, but a contracted tonne is still a promise to perform against a physical supply chain. Pipeline reliability, plant availability, export authorization and customer credit determine how well the contract converts into cash. The 2026 QatarEnergy SPA also makes the conditional nature of some growth support visible: 1 mtpa of the up-to-4 mtpa agreement depends on an SPL Expansion FID and other conditions. [2][3]

The linked purchase and sale positions are one reason the commercial platform can show derivative balances that look larger or move more sharply than the cash economics of a delivered cargo. A fair-value change can enter reported cost of sales before the associated LNG is delivered; later, the physical gas and LNG sale settle under their contract terms. Cheniere's own non-GAAP reconciliations remove qualifying fair-value changes when calculating Adjusted EBITDA, but the GAAP statement still records them. For a unit-economics review, separate the timing of mark-to-market accounting from the eventual physical purchase, liquefaction and customer delivery. [2][3]

Maintenance and weather are operational inputs into the delivery schedule, not afterthoughts. The company reports that production levels and maintenance timing can make operating profit uneven across quarters and that temperature affects facility output. Each train must be balanced with planned downtime, pipeline nominations, storage inventory and marine berth availability. Cheniere's tanks and multiple docks provide useful scheduling flexibility, but no public metric in the cited materials quantifies how much buffer each cargo schedule has in a normal operating quarter. [2][4][5]

book_paragraphs: Let us trace one cargo from the gas field to a customer, because the economics become much clearer when you follow the physical path. A producer sells pipeline gas to Cheniere or an affiliate. The commercial team has to match that supply with transport capacity into Sabine Pass or Corpus Christi. The pipeline system is not owned entirely by Cheniere; access depends in part on contracted service from third parties. Sabine Pass's multiple connections and Corpus Christi's access to Permian and other supply regions diversify the route, but the company still needs a reliable flow of gas into the plant. [2][4][5]

At the terminal, operators remove impurities and cool the feed gas until it condenses into LNG. That liquid is stored in insulated tanks until a carrier is ready to load. A liquefaction train is an industrial process plant, not a passive warehouse: compressors, refrigeration systems, utilities, maintenance, pipeline pressure and ship schedules all have to work together. The product is much denser in liquid form, allowing a ship to transport a volume that would be impractical as uncompressed gas over the same ocean distance. [4][5]

Then the contract decides how the cargo leaves the seller's hands. Under FOB, the buyer takes delivery at the loading terminal and usually provides the vessel. Under DAP, Cheniere can charter the ship and carry the LNG to the buyer's nominated terminal. Petrobras's new agreement is FOB and lasts 22 years for approximately 0.8 million tonnes a year. Its price is not in the public announcement, so we can explain the obligations without guessing the fee or the gas index. [2][3][13]

The pricing structure in Cheniere's 10-K helps separate two economic components. Many long-term SPAs include fixed fees on contracted volumes, generally payable even if the buyer does not lift a cargo, plus variable fees largely indexed to Henry Hub and designed to cover the feed-gas and associated transport and fuel costs. This is not a guarantee that every cost is passed through perfectly. The actual SPA controls, and pipeline constraints, operating performance, fuel use, credit terms and delivery windows can affect realized margins. [2]

IPM contracts add another layer. The producer sells gas to Cheniere using a global LNG or natural-gas index less specified fees and other costs. Cheniere then manages the LNG marketing exposure. Derivatives may manage some of the difference between purchase and sale timing, but GAAP can recognize a fair-value movement before the related physical cargo is delivered. That accounting timing is a reason quarterly earnings can move differently from loaded volume and from cash receipts. In the first nine months of 2026, Cheniere attributed most of its year-over-year GAAP net-income decline to $3.6 billion of unfavorable derivative fair-value variances, largely tied to long-term IPM agreements, even while volumes and Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA increased. [2][3]

Cash conversion also follows contract mechanics. A cargo loaded FOB and a cargo delivered across an ocean do not necessarily reach the same revenue-recognition point. Some delivered volumes can still be in transit on the reporting date. A tiered payment schedule can create a contract asset: Cheniere has transferred goods or service but the right to invoice or collect is not yet unconditional. The Form 10-K disclosed $424 million of contract assets at year-end 2025, and one customer accounted for 15% of combined trade receivables and contract assets even though no customer provided 10% of external revenue. That is why you should examine both income statement diversification and balance-sheet concentration. [2][3]

The audited FY2025 waterfall is the compact way to see the full path. For every $100 of revenue, the company must first absorb the reported operating cost base, then net non-operating expense and tax, before the attributable earnings figure emerges. It generated $5.539 billion of CFO, spent $3.078 billion on capital expenditures and had $2.461 billion of CFO less capex. This is not free cash available without qualification: some growth spending, debt obligations, distributions to noncontrolling owners and working-capital needs still compete for capital. [2]

A contract's fixed-fee and variable-fee pieces do different jobs. The fixed fee can compensate Cheniere for liquefaction capacity reserved under certain contracts, including when a customer chooses not to lift a cargo. The variable component generally tracks feed gas and related services. For the buyer, FOB can offer cargo-destination flexibility, while for Cheniere it means the buyer organizes ocean carriage after loading. Delivered sales can offer a more turnkey service but leave the seller responsible for vessel arrangements and delivery. Public terms vary, so the general design should guide questions rather than serve as a substitute for the SPA. [2]

The procurement relationship begins before the ship reaches the berth. Cheniere maintains a supplier network and arranges transport to each terminal; the sites draw from different pipeline systems and producing regions. This spreads access across sources, but it also leaves the company exposed to outages and constraints on pipelines it does not fully own. A reliable customer promise depends on the whole chain, from producer nomination and pipeline scheduling to train availability and marine loading. [2][4][5]

After the sale, the handoff determines when the commercial obligation is complete. With FOB, loading is the central delivery event; with delivered sales, the vessel voyage and receiving terminal become part of the seller's performance. The 2026 Q3 filing materials showed delivered cargoes still in transit at quarter end, illustrating how the timing of shipment and revenue can cross reporting periods. If a tiered SPA payment has not yet become due, the resulting asset is not the same as an overdue invoice. That distinction matters when evaluating cash conversion. [2][3]

A good operations review follows a cargo across the reporting boundary. Was LNG produced, loaded, transferred to the buyer or still moving under a delivered contract? Was the variable fee earned on delivery, or did a tiered schedule leave some consideration not yet due? Did the gas-purchase derivative mark move before the cargo's sale was recognized? Cheniere's disclosures show that all three situations can coexist in one quarter. You should not compress them into one average revenue-per-tonne metric without the contract and accounting context. [2][3]

The waterfall also makes clear that employee expense is not a separate audited category in the published figures. Cheniere reports operating and maintenance costs, selling, general and administrative expense, depreciation and other cost lines, but the headline total of costs and expenses already includes those components. Treating an undisclosed employee-cost allocation as zero would understate the actual cost of running the terminals; subtracting an estimate would make the historical bridge unreconciled. The right unit-economics presentation preserves the audited aggregate and identifies the disclosure gap. [2]

book_subsections.title: The $100 bridge is a statement reconciliation, not a margin forecast
paragraphs: Use the waterfall as a one-period operating map, not a promise for a future year. The builder scales the actual 2025 audited line items. Employee costs are not separately published in the statement categories, so the correct treatment is to leave them unallocated rather than insert a false zero. D&A of $1.329 billion is embedded in reported operating costs, and interest expense of $948 million contributes to the net non-operating line; adding either again as a new step would double count or fail to reconcile with the published totals. [2]

At the bottom, CFO less capex is $2.461 billion. This is a useful cash measure, but it is not the same as Cheniere's company-defined Distributable Cash Flow. DCF adjusts for maintenance capital, interest, cash tax and noncontrolling interests, while CFO less capex is a simple subtraction from the audited cash-flow statement. Keeping those labels separate protects you from mixing GAAP cash with a management-defined measure. [2][3]

The statement categories also constrain what can be said about the cost of serving one cargo. Operating costs include gas purchases and transport, operating and maintenance, depreciation and other expense, but the audited lines do not allocate all of those costs by contract or train. The 2025 Form 10-K discusses fixed and variable SPA components at a general level, while exact customer terms are proprietary. You can understand the structure and reconcile the consolidated year, but you cannot derive a Petrobras cargo margin from public terms that were not disclosed. [2][3]

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The cargo is the visible product; the contract is the invisible choreography. Cheniere earns its role by coordinating gas, pipelines, a cryogenic plant, storage, a vessel slot and a buyer's receiving system. For you, the key discipline is to follow who owns each cost and risk at each handoff, then reconcile that operational chain to cash rather than assuming the LNG cargo's invoice is the whole story.
